Consult Summary:
- 45-year-old active female runner with ~2 weeks of right knee pain and clicking that begins ~20 minutes into runs after an increase in mileage; intermittent mild swelling initially, currently no resting pain; clinician recommends rest/ice, physiotherapy referral, and a prescription for a stronger oral anti-inflammatory (sent to pharmacy). DDx supports overuse patellofemoral/ITB/meniscal causes.

History:
- Presenting complaint:
  - Right knee pain with audible/subjective clicking for ~2 weeks; reduced tolerance for running.
  - One transient episode of tingling in the right toes after a run.
- Timeline:
  - Symptoms began ~2 weeks ago after increasing running mileage for marathon training (longer runs started ~1 month ago; has done several 7-mile runs).
  - Initial mild swelling after the first long run resolved with ice. Current state: intermittent symptoms provoked by activity; knee not painful at rest during the video call.
  - Pain typically starts ~20 minutes into a run (~2.5–3 miles) and has been worse with recent runs, prompting stopping in the most recent episode.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Aggravated by running and movements requiring repeated knee flexion/extension (e.g., abdominal exercises involving leg straightening).
  - Improved with ice and temporary reduction in activity. Patient takes occasional NSAIDs (ibuprofen/Aleve) for symptoms.
- Associated symptoms / review of systems:
  - Occasional transient toe tingling (right side) after one run; resolved.
  - No locking, no giving-way/instability, no current swelling, no redness or warmth reported.
  - No difficulty walking normally, no problems on stairs, full ability to straighten and flex the knee per patient and clinician assessment.
  - No systemic symptoms (fever, malaise) reported.
- Other relevant factors from history:
  - Prior fall while playing ice hockey months ago resulting in a large bruise; no documented fracture or surgery.
  - Training for a marathon in June; increased running volume recently.

Past Medical History:
- Ophthalmologic: LASIK (date not specified).
- Prior significant event: Emergency evaluation for presumed kidney stone / severe UTI in the past (required ER care; morphine discussion noted).
- Orthopedic/trauma: Ice-hockey fall months ago with marked bruise (no documented formal knee diagnosis).
- Medications (explicitly mentioned; dose/route/frequency not documented unless specified):
  - Vitamin D — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Melatonin — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Ibuprofen — dose/route/frequency not documented (patient stated occasional; usually 400 mg max).
  - Aleve (naproxen assumed by patient) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Xanax (occasional) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Note: Clinician to send a prescription for a stronger anti-inflammatory—prescription sent to pharmacy; dose/route/frequency not documented.
- Allergies: Not documented in transcript.

Social History:
- Lives in London (address provided).
- Highly active: regular gym workouts, ice hockey player, currently training for a marathon.
- Tobacco: No tobacco smoking documented.
- Alcohol: Not documented.
- Recreational drug use: Occasional cannabis use ("smokes a joint").
- Occupation/financial/social supports: Not documented.

Family History:
- Not documented.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: None recorded.
- Exam findings (video/telemedicine assessment and patient report):
  - Right knee: full range of motion (full flexion and extension reported).
  - No current swelling, no warmth, no erythema at time of assessment.
  - No locking or mechanical obstruction reported.
  - No instability/giving way reported.
  - Able to walk and use stairs without difficulty.
  - Note: Examination limited by video/remote format; no hands-on palpation documented.

Investigations:
- No imaging, laboratory tests, or formal orthopedic testing performed or reported.
- No prior imaging or tests referenced in transcript.

Assessment & Plan:
(Integrates clinician impressions from transcript with DDx-supported possibilities)

Issue 1: Overuse patellofemoral pain / patellar maltracking (runner's knee) — primary working diagnosis (supported by clinician assessment and DDx)
- Assessment:
  - Typical history of anterior/knee pain after increasing running mileage, starts after ~20 minutes of running; clicking with flexion/extension; transient swelling after exertion that improved with ice.
  - DDx rates patellofemoral pain syndrome as most likely.
- Plan:
  - Conservative management advised: continue ice therapy as patient already doing.
  - Activity modification: reduce running volume and avoid painful long runs while symptoms persist.
  - Physiotherapy referral arranged/requested for detailed assessment and rehabilitation (strengthening, patellar tracking exercises, gait/running form review).
  - Prescription for a "slightly stronger" oral anti-inflammatory sent to pharmacy (dose/route/frequency not documented). Counsel patient to:
    - Not combine this prescription with existing ibuprofen.
    - Take with food to reduce GI risk.
  - If symptoms persist or fail to improve with physiotherapy, consider orthopedic review and imaging (e.g., MRI) to evaluate cartilage/patellofemoral joint — imaging only if indicated after assessment.
  - Follow-up: return to clinic or physiotherapist as arranged; patient instructed to seek urgent review earlier if red-flag signs develop.

Issue 2: Lateral knee overuse/IT band syndrome or patellar tendinopathy — alternative overuse diagnoses (supported by DDx)
- Assessment:
  - DDx lists IT band syndrome (medium likelihood) and patellar tendinopathy (low–medium) as possible causes given running-related onset and pain location variability (patient reported pain shifting slightly to the right/lateral).
- Plan:
  - Addressed within physiotherapy assessment and rehabilitation (targeted stretching/strengthening, foam rolling, load management).
  - Modify training (reduce mileage, cross-train) to offload implicated structures.
  - Analgesia as above (NSAID prescription or OTC NSAIDs as tolerated/use per guidance).

Issue 3: Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury — possible given prior trauma and clicking (DDx medium likelihood)
- Assessment:
  - Prior ice-hockey fall months ago could have caused meniscal/cartilage injury that is now symptomatic with increased loading. Lack of locking or persistent swelling and preserved ROM make a large mechanical meniscal tear less likely but cannot be excluded.
- Plan:
  - Clinical assessment by physiotherapist/orthopedist to assess for focal joint line tenderness, mechanical symptoms; if exam suggests internal derangement or if refractory to conservative care, obtain MRI for evaluation.
  - Continue activity modification and symptomatic care in the interim.

Issue 4: Transient exertional nerve irritation/peripheral neuropathy — explains one episode of toe tingling (DDx low–moderate)
- Assessment:
  - One-time transient right toe tingling after a run; no ongoing neurologic deficits, no color/temperature change, no calf pain.
- Plan:
  - Monitor for recurrence. If persistent or progressive paresthesia, obtain focused neurologic exam and consider further testing (nerve conduction study or imaging) if clinically indicated.

Safety / Red flags (explicitly stated to patient in transcript):
- Patient advised to seek urgent care and contact clinic if new or persistent findings occur:
  - Persistent or worsening swelling, redness, heat of knee, systemic symptoms/fever, or inability to bend/straighten the knee (locking).
  - If appointment with physiotherapy is delayed and symptoms worsen, patient can be seen in clinic earlier.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- 1) Patellofemoral pain syndrome / patellar maltracking — High likelihood
  - Reasoning: Classic overuse pattern in a runner after increased mileage; activity-related anterior knee pain starting after ~20 minutes; clicking with flexion/extension; transient swelling responding to ice.
- 2) Iliotibial band (ITB) syndrome or lateral tendinopathy — Moderate likelihood
  - Reasoning: Timing of pain during runs (after a period of exertion) and patient's description of pain shifting laterally are consistent; lack of focal lateral tenderness on exam (not assessed fully) tempers certainty.
- 3) Meniscal or intra-articular cartilage injury — Moderate likelihood
  - Reasoning: Intermittent clicking and prior trauma (ice-hockey fall) raise concern for meniscal or chondral lesion; absence of locking, persistent swelling, or focal joint-line tenderness on remote exam reduces likelihood but does not exclude it.
- Additional from DDx: DVT considered but Low likelihood given lack of calf pain, persistent unilateral swelling, warmth, erythema, or systemic signs.

Quality checks (document_quality):
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Allergies not documented.
  - No formal vital signs recorded.
  - No focused in-person musculoskeletal exam findings (palpation, specific special tests such as patellar grind, McMurray, joint-line tenderness) — limited by telemedicine.
  - No imaging or labs performed or available.
  - Exact prescription details (drug name/dose/route/frequency) for the stronger anti-inflammatory were not documented.
  - No documentation of whether a physiotherapy referral appointment was scheduled (timing/location).
  - No tobacco/alcohol frequency quantified beyond recreational cannabis use.
- Conflicts between transcript and DDx:
  - None significant; DDx aligns with transcript history and clinician impression. (If present: "conflict noted" — not applicable.)
- Transcript quality:
  - Audio/video adequate for history taking; some conversational fillers and brief uncertainty (patient unsure about Aleve class or drug names).
  - Physical exam limited by remote format; clinician documented functional testing (range of motion, ability to use stairs) but no hands-on exam.
